analysis.one_liner: Loosens federal oversight of banks, savings institutions, and credit unions — easing lending limits, reporting rules, and examination requirements.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 415–2 on March 8, 2006, but the Senate Banking Committee never acted on it before that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite banking law to give banks, savings and loan institutions, and credit unions more freedom: higher caps on commercial real estate and business lending, an end to statutory dividend formulas, fewer required reports on loans to bank insiders, less frequent examinations for larger banks, and streamlined merger reviews. It also includes a handful of provisions aimed at ordinary people, like letting credit unions offer longer loans and money-transfer services and giving community-reinvestment credit for employee ownership plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Depository institutions are the main beneficiaries. National banks gain easier dividend rules and fewer insider-lending reports; savings associations gain expanded authority to make commercial, auto, and small business loans and to merge with nondepository affiliates; finance companies gain the ability to charge the same maximum interest rates as banks; credit unions gain longer loan terms, larger investments, and money-transfer authority. Community banks and credit unions also gain lighter reporting burdens.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the cap on commercial real estate loans by a federal savings association from 400% to 500% of its capital, and removes a limit on how large a single residential development loan can be [S3].
Repeals specified federal reporting requirements on loans made to bank executive officers and principal shareholders, reducing disclosure of insider lending [S3].

Lets federal credit unions make loans with terms up to 15 years instead of 12, offer money transfer and check-cashing services to people in their field of membership, and invest more in credit union service organizations [S3].

Allows savings associations to make investments promoting the public welfare of low- and moderate-income communities, and adds community reinvestment credit for supporting employee stock ownership plans and worker-owned cooperatives [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Deposit insurance funds and depositors bear more of the risk if looser lending and lighter oversight lead to failures. Borrowers who use finance companies could pay more, since the bill lets those lenders charge the same maximum rates as banks. The public also gets less visibility into bank insider lending.

drawbacks.text: Repealing insider-lending reporting requirements removes a transparency tool that lets regulators and the public track loans to bank executives and major shareholders [S3].

The bill permits finance companies to charge the same maximum annual interest rates as national and state banks, removing a rate distinction that had applied to credit sales and financing transactions [S3].
It limits new multi-agency guidance on credit card minimum payments and negative amortization so that it does not apply to balances that already existed when the bill took effect [S3].

Larger banks (up to $1 billion in assets) would qualify for an 18-month examination cycle instead of more frequent onsite exams, and federal banking agencies could waive examination schedules generally [S3].
National bank directors could declare dividends of undivided profits 'as they judge to be expedient,' replacing the statutory formula that tied dividends to profits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a broad deregulatory package for depository institutions. Its lighter-touch provisions — community-development investing authority, credit union member services, employee-ownership credit — are real but secondary to the main thrust, which relaxes lending limits, oversight frequency, and disclosure rules on the theory that regulation of healthy banks is too burdensome. An honest supporter would acknowledge that loosened lending caps, reduced insider-lending reporting, and fewer examinations shift risk onto the deposit insurance system, while the consumer-facing gains are modest.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it nearly unanimously under a fast-track procedure, but the Senate Banking Committee — where it was referred the day after — never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Financial Services Committee reported the bill amended on December 17, 2005, by a vote of 109-356 Part I after the full committee approved it 67-0 in markup [S1][S8].
The House Judiciary Committee also reported the bill on February 16, 2006, clearing it for floor action [S1][S8].

On March 8, 2006, the House passed the bill under suspension of the rules — a fast-track process requiring a two-thirds majority — by 415 to 2, with 193 of 201 voting Democrats and 221 of 230 voting Republicans in favor [S8][S9].

The next day, March 9, 2006, the Senate received the bill and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where no further action appears in the record before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S8].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Neither side gained much. Depository institutions remained subject to the existing lending limits, reporting rules, and examination schedules, but the bill's consumer protections — such as the ban on interstate branching by commercial-firm-owned industrial loan companies and FDIC authority over golden parachute payments — also never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held for banks and public alike

for.what_they_did: Voted to pass the bill 415-2, with only one Democrat and one Republican voting no [S9].

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors — 15 Democrats and 24 Republicans [S7].

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was overwhelmingly bipartisan — 193 of 201 voting Democrats and 221 of 230 voting Republicans voted yes, with just two no votes total [S9].

industries.note: The bill raises lending caps, eases dividend rules, repeals insider-lending reporting, and lengthens examination cycles — trading oversight burden for more bank flexibility, with the residual risk falling on depositors and the insurance system [S3].

Credit unions gain longer loan terms, wider investment authority, money-transfer services, and easier mergers — powers that flow to their member-owners, though lighter net-worth rules also loosen safety margins [S3].

By extending the bank interest-rate provision to credit sales and financing transactions, the bill lets finance companies charge the same maximum rates as banks, which can mean higher borrowing costs for consumers [S3].

industries.industry: Bad-check enforcement and debt collection firms
industries.note: The bill exempts state-supervised private bad-check enforcement programs from Fair Debt Collection Practices Act oversight, removing a layer of federal consumer protection from those programs [S3].
